Splitting the difference: Computations of the Reynolds operator
in classical invariant theoryThanks: The author was supported by NSF grants DMS 2101671 and DMS 2349623.

Aryaman Maithani Address: Department of Mathematics, University of Utah, 155 South 1400 East, Salt Lake City, UT 84112, USA Email address: maithani@math.utah.edu
Abstract.

If GG is a linearly reductive group acting rationally on a polynomial ring SS, then the inclusion SG​⸦-→SS^{G}\lhook\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow S possesses a unique GG-equivariant splitting, called the Reynolds operator. We describe algorithms for computing the Reynolds operator for the classical actions as in Weyl’s book. The groups are the general linear group, the special linear group, the orthogonal group, and the symplectic group, with their classical representations: direct sums of copies of the standard representation and copies of the dual representation.

Key words and phrases: 
Reynolds operator, ring of invariants, classical groups, linearly reductive groups.

1. Introduction

Consider a group GG acting on a ring SS by ring automorphisms. The ring of invariants for this group action is defined as

SG≔{s∈S:g⁡(s)=g​for all​g∈G},S^{G}\coloneqq\{s\in S:g(s)=g\ \text{for all}\ g\in G\},

that is, SGS^{G} is the subring of elements that are fixed by each group element. We have the inclusion of rings

(1.1) SG​⸦-→S.S^{G}\lhook\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow S.

The above is also then an inclusion of SGS^{G}-modules. A natural question to ask is whether Equation 1.1 splits in the category of SGS^{G}-modules — in which case SGS^{G} is a direct summand of SS. A positive answer to this question often implies good properties about the subring; for example, a direct summand of a noetherian ring is again noetherian. A deeper result is the Hochster–Roberts theorem [HR], which states that a direct summand of a polynomial ring is Cohen–Macaulay. The inclusion Equation 1.1 does not always split; a simple example is the alternating group A3A_{3} acting on 𝔽3​[x,y,z]\mathbb{F}_{3}[x,y,z] by permuting the variables, see Example 4.4. A more dramatic example was given by \CiteauthorNagarajan [Na], where a group of order two acts on a regular ring for which the ring of invariants is not noetherian. For finite groups, a simple condition that ensures the existence of a splitting is having order invertible in SS; the inclusion Equation 1.1 then splits with an SGS^{G}-linear splitting given by

s⟼1|G|​∑g∈Sg⁡(s).s\longmapsto\frac{1}{{\left\lvert G\right\lvert}}\sum_{g\in S}g(s).

The above is the Reynolds operator and has the additional property of being GG-equivariant (Definition 2.1).

In this paper, our groups of interest are certain linear algebraic groups over a field kk, that is, Zariski-closed subgroups of GLn⁡(k)\GL_{n}(k). If such a group GG acts (rationally) on a kk-vector space VV, then we get a (rational) degree-preserving kk-algebra action of GG on the polynomial ring S≔Sym⁡(V)S\coloneqq\Sym(V). Hilbert’s fourteenth problem asked if SGS^{G} is always a finitely generated kk-algebra — a question answered in the negative by \CiteauthorNagata14th [Naa] by giving an example where SGS^{G} is not noetherian. For linear algebraic groups, the analogue to having invertible order is to be linearly reductive. These groups admit a similar Reynolds operator, see Theorem 4.2; in particular, the inclusion Equation 1.1 splits GG-equivariantly and SGS^{G}-linearly.

We focus on the following titular classical groups of Weyl’s book [We]: the general linear group GLn⁡(k)\GL_{n}(k), the special linear group SLn⁡(k)\SL_{n}(k), the orthogonal group On⁡(k)\OO_{n}(k), and the symplectic group Sp2​n⁡(k)\Sp_{2n}(k). As in the book, we look at their classical actions, corresponding to the direct sum of copies of the standard representation and possibly copies of the dual representation. We record the rings of invariants for some of these actions in Theorem 3.1. This includes infinite fields of positive characteristic as in [DP, Hab]. There is, however, a stark difference between characteristics zero and positive: if kk is a field of characteristic zero, then the groups listed above are all linearly reductive. This is typically not the case in positive characteristic wherein these groups admit representations for which the ring of invariants is not Cohen–Macaulay [Ko]. Moreover — while the classical rings of invariants continue to be Cohen–Macaulay even in positive characteristic — the inclusion Equation 1.1 is rarely split [HJPS]. This has the interesting consequence that given any splitting over ℚ\mathbb{Q}, every prime must appear in the denominator of the image of any basis; see Remark 8.3 for a precise statement.

For the most part, we consider these classical groups in characteristic zero. Because these are then linearly reductive, the inclusion Equation 1.1 splits. We give an algorithm for explicitly computing the Reynolds operator in each case in terms of certain integrals of monomial functions. We do this by reducing the computation to one over a compact Lie group, in which case we may integrate with respect to the Haar measure akin to averaging over a finite group. Methods to compute these integrals are of interest in mathematical physics due to their important role in areas such as mesoscopic transport, quantum chaos, and quantum information and decoherence. This interest has led to the development of various algorithms — such as the invariant method and the column vector method — to compute these integrals; see the introduction of [GL] for more on this topic.

We remark that there are conditions weaker than having invertible order or being linearly reductive that imply finite generation of SGS^{G}. Indeed, Noether [No] showed that if GG is a finite group acting on a finitely generated kk-algebra SS by kk-algebra automorphisms, then SGS^{G} is a finitely generated kk-algebra. Similarly, \CiteauthorHaboush:Reductive [Ha] proved that if GG is a reductive group acting rationally on a finitely generated kk-algebra SS, then SGS^{G} is finitely generated. While the classical groups are no longer linearly reductive in positive characteristic, they continue to be reductive, and hence the invariant subrings are known to be finitely generated.

The paper is arranged as follows. After setting up the notations and definitions in Section 2, we define the classical group actions in Section 3 and record the rings of invariants. In Section 4, we recall the relevant facts about linearly reductive groups. Section 5 discusses the computation of the Reynolds operator for a compact Lie group. We discuss facts about the Haar measure and set up the required machinery to integrate functions that take values in polynomial rings. Section 6 begins by describing how the computation of the Reynolds operator for a classical group over an arbitrary field of characteristic zero can be reduced to that for a compact Lie group. With this reduction in place, we then give algorithms that one may implement on a computer algebra system. We make use of these algorithms in Section 7 to provide explicit formulae for the Reynolds operators for the SL\SL and GL\GL actions. These algorithms have been implemented in SageMath [Th], and we note some conjectures arising out of these computations. Lastly, we compare with the situation in positive characteristic in Section 8.

2. Notations and definitions

The letter kk will denote a field. For n⩾1n\geqslant 1, 𝔸kn\mathbb{A}_{k}^{n} denotes the topological space knk^{n} with the Zariski topology. We recall the following classical groups of invertible matrices.

  1. (a)

    (General linear group) GLn⁡(k)\GL_{n}(k) is the group of n×nn\times n invertible matrices over kk.

  2. (b)

    (Special linear group) SLn⁡(k)≔{M∈GLn⁡(k):det(M)=1}\SL_{n}(k)\coloneqq\{M\in\GL_{n}(k):\det(M)=1\}.

  3. (c)

    (Orthogonal group) On⁡(k)≔{M∈GLn⁡(k):Mtr​M=In}\OO_{n}(k)\coloneqq\{M\in\GL_{n}(k):M^{\operatorname{tr}}M=I_{n}\}, where InI_{n} denotes the identity matrix.

  4. (d)

    (Symplectic group) Sp2​n⁡(k)≔{M∈GL2​n⁡(k):Mtr​Ω​M=Ω}\Sp_{2n}(k)\coloneqq\{M\in\GL_{2n}(k):M^{\operatorname{tr}}\Omega M=\Omega\}, where Ω≔(OIn−InO)\Omega\coloneqq\left(\begin{smallmatrix}O&I_{n}\\ -I_{n}&O\\ \end{smallmatrix}\right).

When the field kk is taken to be the complex numbers, we have the following additional subgroups.

  1. (e)

    (Unitary group) Un⁡(ℂ)≔{U∈GLn⁡(ℂ):U​U∗=In}\UU_{n}(\mathbb{C})\coloneqq\{U\in\GL_{n}(\mathbb{C}):UU^{\ast}=I_{n}\}, where U∗U^{\ast} denotes the conjugate transpose of UU.

  2. (f)

    (Special unitary group) SUn⁡(ℂ)≔Un⁡(ℂ)∩SLn⁡(ℂ)\SU_{n}(\mathbb{C})\coloneqq\UU_{n}(\mathbb{C})\cap\SL_{n}(\mathbb{C}).

  3. (g)

    (Symplectic unitary group) SpU2​n⁡(ℂ)≔U2​n⁡(ℂ)∩Sp2​n⁡(ℂ)\SpU_{2n}(\mathbb{C})\coloneqq\UU_{2n}(\mathbb{C})\cap\Sp_{2n}(\mathbb{C}).

All the above groups inherit the subspace topology from 𝔸kn2\mathbb{A}_{k}^{n^{2}}, and we refer to this as the Zariski topology. These are all topological groups — though typically not Hausdorff — because the product and inversion functions are continuous in the Zariski topology, being given by rational functions in the entries of the matrices.

When k=ℂk=\mathbb{C}, these groups also have the Euclidean topology and moreover are smooth submanifolds of ℂn2\mathbb{C}^{n^{2}}. In this case, the product and inversion functions are smooth; hence, these are all Lie groups.

Definition 2.1.

Let GG be a group acting by ring automorphisms on a ring SS. A splitting for the inclusion SG​⸦-→SS^{G}\lhook\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow S is an additive function ℛ:S-→SG\mathcal{R}\colon S\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow S^{G} such that ℛ⁡(r)=r\mathcal{R}(r)=r for all r∈SGr\in S^{G}. The splitting is GG-equivariant if ℛ⁡(g⁡(s))=ℛ⁡(s)\mathcal{R}(g(s))=\mathcal{R}(s) for all g∈Gg\in G and s∈Ss\in S. The splitting is SGS^{G}-linear if ℛ⁡(r​s)=r​ℛ​(s)\mathcal{R}(rs)=r\mathcal{R}(s) for all r∈SGr\in S^{G} and s∈Ss\in S.

3. The classical group actions

Let kk be a field, and tt, mm, nn be positive integers. We use the notation

k[Yt×n]≔k[yi​j:1⩽i⩽t, 1⩽j⩽n],k[Y_{t\times n}]\coloneqq k[y_{ij}:1\leqslant i\leqslant t,\,1\leqslant j\leqslant n],

that is, k⁡[Yt×n]k[Y_{t\times n}] is a polynomial ring over kk in t​ntn variables. Once the dimensions have been specified, we write k⁡[Y]k[Y] for brevity. We use the letter YY for the t×nt\times n matrix [yi​j]i,j[y_{ij}]_{i,j}. The notation naturally extends to k⁡[Xm×t,Yt×n]k[X_{m\times t},Y_{t\times n}].

Let GG be one of the groups GLt⁡(k)\GL_{t}(k), SLt⁡(k)\SL_{t}(k), Ot⁡(k)\OO_{t}(k), or Spt⁡(k)\Sp_{t}(k), where for the last case, we assume that tt is even. We will consider the following two types of rational actions of GG.

  1. (R1)

    The group GG acts on k⁡[Yt×n]k[Y_{t\times n}], where the action of M∈GM\in G is given by

    M:Y⟼M​Y;M\colon Y\longmapsto MY;

    by the above, we mean that [Y]i​j⟼[M​Y]i​j[Y]_{ij}\longmapsto[MY]_{ij}.

  2. (R2)

    The group GG acts on k⁡[Xm×t,Yt×n]k[X_{m\times t},Y_{t\times n}], where the action of M∈GM\in G is given by

    M:{X⟼X​M−1,Y⟼M​Y.M\colon\begin{cases}X\longmapsto XM^{-1},\\ Y\longmapsto MY.\end{cases}

The first action corresponds to the direct sum of nn copies of the standard representation, whereas the second has an additional mm copies of the dual representation. We will describe the splittings for all of these actions.

We recall below the classical rings of invariants as in Weyl’s book [We] where they were originally discussed in characteristic zero. A characteristic-free proof of the following theorem can be found in [DP, Hab].

Theorem 3.1.

Let kk be an infinite field. With the above actions, we have the following rings of invariants.

  1. (a)

    (General linear group) For positive integers tt, mm, nn, the equality

    k​[Xm×t,Yt×n]GLt⁡(k)=k⁡[X​Y]k[X_{m\times t},Y_{t\times n}]^{\GL_{t}(k)}=k[XY]

    holds, that is, the invariant ring is generated, as a kk-algebra, by the entries of the matrix product X​YXY.

  2. (b)

    (Special linear group) For positive integers tt, nn with t⩽nt\leqslant n, the equality

    k​[Yt×n]SLt⁡(k)=k⁡[size t minors]k[Y_{t\times n}]^{\SL_{t}(k)}=k[\text{size $t$ minors}]

    holds, that is, the invariant ring is generated, as a kk-algebra, by the size tt minors of the matrix YY.

  3. (c)

    (Orthogonal group) For positive integers tt, nn and char⁡(k)≠2\chr(k)\neq 2, the equality

    k​[Yt×n]Ot⁡(k)=k⁡[Ytr​Y]k[Y_{t\times n}]^{\OO_{t}(k)}=k[Y^{\operatorname{tr}}Y]

    holds, that is, the invariant ring is generated, as a kk-algebra, by the entries of the matrix product Ytr​YY^{\operatorname{tr}}Y.

  4. (d)

    (Symplectic group) For positive integers tt, nn, the equality

    k​[Y2​t×n]Sp2​t⁡(k)=k⁡[Ytr​Ω​Y]k[Y_{2t\times n}]^{\Sp_{2t}(k)}=k[Y^{\operatorname{tr}}\Omega Y]

    holds, that is, the invariant ring is generated, as a kk-algebra, by the entries of the matrix product Ytr​Ω​YY^{\operatorname{tr}}\Omega Y.

Remark 3.2.

For each of the above actions, the fixed subring is of independent interest for the reasons described below. We denote the invariant subring in the respective cases by RR.

  1. (a)

    (General linear group) The ring RR is isomorphic to the determinantal ring k⁡[Zm×n]/It+1​(Z)k[Z_{m\times n}]/I_{t+1}(Z), where It+1​(Z)I_{t+1}(Z) is the ideal generated by the size t+1t+1 minors of ZZ.

  2. (b)

    (Special linear group) The ring RR is the Plücker coordinate ring of the Grassmannian of tt-dimensional subspaces of an nn-dimensional space.

  3. (c)

    (Orthogonal group) The ring RR is isomorphic to k​[Z]/It+1​(Z)k[Z]/I_{t+1}(Z), where ZZ is an n×nn\times n symmetric matrix of indeterminates.

  4. (d)

    (Symplectic group) The ring RR is isomorphic to k⁡[Z]/Pf2​t+2⁡(Z)k[Z]/\Pf_{2t+2}(Z), where ZZ is an n×nn\times n alternating matrix of indeterminates, and Pf2​t+2⁡(Z)\Pf_{2t+2}(Z) the ideal generated by its principal (2​t+2)(2t+2)-Pfaffians.

4. Linearly reductive groups

This section contextualises our results with the broader theory of linearly reductive groups. For the most part, this is only for theoretical interest, as we will compute the Reynolds operator concretely by integrating over a compact Lie group. For an introduction to linear algebraic groups and rational actions, we refer the reader to one of [Fo, Mu, Ho, DK]. We record the relevant facts here.

Definition 4.1.

Let GG be a linear algebraic group over the field kk, and VV a rational representation of GG. A Reynolds operator is a kk-linear, GG-equivariant splitting ℛ:k⁡[V]-→k​[V]G\mathcal{R}\colon k[V]\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow k[V]^{G}.

Theorem 4.2.

If GG is linearly reductive, then for every rational representation VV, there exists a unique Reynolds operator ℛ:k⁡[V]-→k​[V]G\mathcal{R}\colon k[V]\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow k[V]^{G}. Moreover, ℛ\mathcal{R} is k​[V]Gk[V]^{G}-linear.

Proof.

The statements are Theorem 2.2.5 and Corollary 2.2.7 in [DK], respectively. ∎

Example 4.3.

We give an example of a group GG acting on a polynomial ring SS for which there exists an SGS^{G}-linear splitting but no GG-equivariant splitting. Let GG be the symmetric group on two element, and S≔𝔽2​[x,y]S\coloneqq\mathbb{F}_{2}[x,y]. The group GG acts on SS by permuting the variables, and the invariant subring is 𝔽2​[x+y,x​y]\mathbb{F}_{2}[x+y,xy]. Because SS is a free SGS^{G}-module with {1,x}\{1,x\} as a basis, the inclusion SG​⸦-→SS^{G}\lhook\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow S splits SGS^{G}-linearly. Suppose that π:S-→SG\pi\colon S\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow S^{G} is a GG-equivariant splitting. Then, π⁡(x)=π⁡(y)\pi(x)=\pi(y) because xx and yy are in the same orbit. But then,

x+y=π⁡(x+y)=π⁡(x)+π⁡(y)=2​π​(x)=0,x+y=\pi(x+y)=\pi(x)+\pi(y)=2\pi(x)=0,

a contradiction. Thus, SG​⸦-→SS^{G}\lhook\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow S admits no GG-equivariant splitting even though it splits SGS^{G}-linearly. This example extends mutatis mutandis to any positive characteristic pp by considering the permutation action of Σp\Sigma_{p} — the symmetric group on pp elements — on the polynomial ring 𝔽p​[x1,…,xp]\mathbb{F}_{p}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{p}].

Example 4.4.

We now give an example of a group action for which no SGS^{G}-linear splitting exists. Consider the action of the alternating group G≔A3G\coloneqq A_{3} on the polynomial ring S≔𝔽3​[x,y,z]S\coloneqq\mathbb{F}_{3}[x,y,z] by permuting the variables. If we let e1e_{1}, e2e_{2}, e3e_{3} denote the elementary symmetric polynomials in xx, yy, zz and set Δ≔(x−y)​(y−z)​(z−x)\Delta\coloneqq(x-y)(y-z)(z-x), then one can check that Δ∈SG\Delta\in S^{G}, Δ∉(e1,e2,e3)​SG\Delta\notin(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})S^{G}, but Δ∈(e1,e2,e3)​S\Delta\in(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})S. This implies that SG​⸦-→SS^{G}\lhook\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow S does not split over SGS^{G}. More generally, if AnA_{n} acts on S=𝔽p​[x1,…,xn]S=\mathbb{F}_{p}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] by permuting variables, the inclusion SAn​⸦-→SS^{A_{n}}\lhook\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow S splits if and only if pp does not divide |An|{\left\lvert A_{n}\right\lvert}; the nontrivial implication was proven in [Gl, Theorem 12.2] for p∤n⁡(n−1)p\nmid n(n-1), and the general case can be found in [Si, Theorem 5.5], [Sm], [Je, Theorem 2.18], and [GJS, Corollary 4.2].

Example 4.5.

If kk is a field of characteristic zero, then the classical groups GLn⁡(k)\GL_{n}(k), SLn⁡(k)\SL_{n}(k), On⁡(k)\OO_{n}(k), and Sp2​n⁡(k)\Sp_{2n}(k) are all linearly reductive, as are all finite groups. For a finite group GG, the Reynolds operator is just averaging over the group: ℛ⁡(f)=1|G|​∑g∈Gg⁡(f)\mathcal{R}(f)=\frac{1}{{\left\lvert G\right\lvert}}\sum\limits_{g\in G}g(f).

The above Reynolds operator extends naturally to smooth actions of a compact Lie group; see Theorem 5.6. The following theorem, in conjunction with Proposition 6.4, tells us how the computation of the Reynolds operator for a linearly reductive group over ℂ\mathbb{C} can be reduced to that for a compact Lie group.

Theorem 4.6.

Let GG be a linear algebraic group over ℂ\mathbb{C}. The following are equivalent.

  1. (a)

    GG is linearly reductive.

  2. (b)

    GG has a Zariski-dense subgroup that is a compact Lie group (in the Euclidean topology).

We shall deduce the above theorem for the classical groups of interest by producing Zariski-dense subgroups in Theorem 6.1.

5. The Reynolds operator for a Lie group

We will now describe the Reynolds operator for a compact Lie group acting on a polynomial ring. Strictly speaking, the term “Reynolds operator” was defined for the rational action of a linear algebraic group, but we continue to use this term to mean a (ℂ\mathbb{C}-)linear GG-equivariant splitting. We first recall some theory of integration over such a group.

In this section, a finite-dimensional vector space over ℝ\mathbb{R} will have its canonical structure of a real differentiable manifold. Examples include ℂ\mathbb{C} and finite-dimensional vector spaces over ℂ\mathbb{C}. Let GG be a compact real Lie group and d​G{\mathrm{d}}G denote the (normalised) Haar measure on GG. Given an element g∈Gg\in G, we denote by LgL_{g} and RgR_{g} the left and right translation maps:

(5.1) Lg:G-→G,h⟼g​h,Rg:G-→G,h⟼h​g.\begin{aligned} L_{g}\colon G&\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow G,\\ h&\longmapsto gh,\end{aligned}\qquad\qquad\begin{aligned} R_{g}\colon G&\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow G,\\ h&\longmapsto hg.\end{aligned}

For an introduction to the Haar measure, we refer the reader to one of [Haa, Ro, La]. We next recall the properties of interest to us.

Theorem 5.1.

Let ψ:G-→ℝ\psi\colon G\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} be smooth, and g∈Gg\in G. Then,

∫Gψ​𝑑G=∫G(ψ∘Lg)​𝑑G=∫G(ψ∘Rg)​𝑑G.\int_{G}\psi\,{\mathrm{d}}G=\int_{G}(\psi\circ L_{g})\,{\mathrm{d}}G=\int_{G}(\psi\circ R_{g})\,{\mathrm{d}}G.

If ψ\psi is constant and takes the value 11, then

∫Gψ​𝑑G=1.\int_{G}\psi\,{\mathrm{d}}G=1.

We may naturally extend the integration of scalar-valued functions to vector-valued functions:

Definition 5.2.

Let VV be a finite-dimensional ℝ\mathbb{R}-vector space, and ψ:G-→V\psi\colon G\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow V a smooth function. Fix a basis {v1,…,vn}\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{n}\} of VV. Let ψi:G-→ℝ\psi_{i}\colon G\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} be the corresponding coordinate functions, satisfying ψ⁡(g)=∑ψi​(g)​vi\psi(g)=\sum\psi_{i}(g)v_{i}. We define

∫Gψ≔∑i=1n(∫Gψi​𝑑G)​vi∈V.\int_{G}\psi\coloneqq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\int_{G}\psi_{i}\,{\mathrm{d}}G\right)v_{i}\in V.

One checks that the above definition is independent of the choice of basis. Note that our notation above drops the “d​G{\mathrm{d}}G” when integrating vector-valued functions. This is for ease of notation as we will always be integrating with respect to the Haar measure. The linearity of scalar integration and the properties of the Haar measure readily extend to the following.

Then,

Let ψ:G-→V\psi\colon G\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow V be smooth, and g∈Gg\in G. Then,

Let S=ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]S=\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] be a polynomial ring, and let [S]1[S]_{1} denote the ℂ\mathbb{C}-vector space of homogeneous degree one polynomials. There is a natural isomorphism of groups

{degree-preserving ℂ-algebra automorphisms of S}⟷{ℂ-linear automorphisms of [S]1}.\{\text{degree-preserving $\mathbb{C}$-algebra automorphisms of $S$}\}\longleftrightarrow\{\text{$\mathbb{C}$-linear automorphisms of $[S]_{1}$}\}.

A degree-preserving ℂ\mathbb{C}-algebra action of GG on SS is called smooth if the corresponding action G×[S]1-→[S]1G\times[S]_{1}\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow[S]_{1} is smooth. In this case, the corresponding action G×[S]d-→[S]dG\times[S]_{d}\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow[S]_{d} is smooth for all d⩾0d\geqslant 0, where [S]d[S]_{d} denotes the space of homogeneous polynomials of degree dd. For f∈Sf\in S, define the orbit map

ψf:G\displaystyle\psi_{f}\colon G -→S\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow S
g\displaystyle g ⟼g⁡(f).\displaystyle\longmapsto g(f).

The function ψf\psi_{f} takes values within a finite-dimensional subspace of SS, for example, the space of polynomials of degree at most the degree of ff. If the GG-action is smooth, then ψf\psi_{f} is a smooth function.

Theorem 5.6.

Let GG be a compact Lie group acting smoothly on the polynomial ring S≔ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]S\coloneqq\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] by degree-preserving ℂ\mathbb{C}-algebra automorphisms. Then, SG​⸦-→SS^{G}\lhook\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow S splits with a degree-preserving, GG-equivariant, SGS^{G}-linear splitting ℛ:S-↠SG\mathcal{R}\colon S\relbar\joinrel\twoheadrightarrow S^{G} given by

ℛ:f⟼∫Gψf.\mathcal{R}\colon f\longmapsto\int_{G}\psi_{f}.

Suggestively, the above may be written as

ℛ⁡(f)=∫g∈Gg⁡(f),\mathcal{R}(f)=\int_{g\in G}g(f),

resembling the Reynolds operator for finite groups.

Proof.

The ℂ\mathbb{C}-linearity of ℛ\mathcal{R} is clear. If ff is homogeneous, then ψf\psi_{f} takes values in subspace [S]deg⁡(f)[S]_{\deg(f)} and in turn, ℛ⁡(f)∈[S]deg⁡(f)\mathcal{R}(f)\in[S]_{\deg(f)}. Thus, ℛ\mathcal{R} is a degree-preserving ℂ\mathbb{C}-linear map.

For the rest of the proof, we will make repeated use of 5.3 and 5.4. Recall that LgL_{g} and RgR_{g} denote the translation maps, defined in Equation 5.1. For f∈Sf\in S and g∈Gg\in G, we define the ℂ\mathbb{C}-linear functions S→ρfSS\xrightarrow{\rho_{f}}S and S→μgSS\xrightarrow{\mu_{g}}S given by left multiplication and the GG-action, respectively. Consequently,

ℛ⁡(f)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}(f) =∫Gψf=∫Gψf∘Rg=∫Gψg⁡(f)=ℛ⁡(g⁡(f))\displaystyle=\int_{G}\psi_{f}=\int_{G}\psi_{f}\circ R_{g}=\int_{G}\psi_{g(f)}=\mathcal{R}(g(f))
=∫Gψf∘Lg=∫Gμg∘ψf=μg​(∫Gψf)=g⁡(ℛ⁡(f)).\displaystyle=\int_{G}\psi_{f}\circ L_{g}=\int_{G}\mu_{g}\circ\psi_{f}=\mu_{g}\left(\int_{G}\psi_{f}\right)=g(\mathcal{R}(f)).

The above shows that ℛ\mathcal{R} takes values in SGS^{G} and is GG-equivariant. Lastly, if f∈SGf\in S^{G} and h∈Sh\in S, then

ℛ⁡(f​h)=∫Gψf​h=∫Gρf∘ψh=ρf​(∫Gψh)=f​ℛ​(h),\mathcal{R}(fh)=\int_{G}\psi_{fh}=\int_{G}\rho_{f}\circ\psi_{h}=\rho_{f}\left(\int_{G}\psi_{h}\right)=f\mathcal{R}(h),

and ψf\psi_{f} is identically equal to ff, giving us

ℛ⁡(f)=∫Gψf=f.\mathcal{R}(f)=\int_{G}\psi_{f}=f.

This finishes the proof that ℛ\mathcal{R} is an SGS^{G}-linear splitting. ∎

6. The Reynolds operator for the classical actions

Fix an integer t⩾1t\geqslant 1 and let G⁡(−)\GG(-) be one of GLt⁡(−)\GL_{t}(-), SLt⁡(−)\SL_{t}(-), Ot⁡(−)\OO_{t}(-), or Spt⁡(−)\Sp_{t}(-), where we assume that tt is even in the last case. Define C≔G⁡(ℂ)∩Ut⁡(ℂ)C\coloneqq\GG(\mathbb{C})\cap\UU_{t}(\mathbb{C}). The intersections in the respective cases are Un⁡(ℂ)\UU_{n}(\mathbb{C}), SUn⁡(ℂ)\SU_{n}(\mathbb{C}), On⁡(ℝ)\OO_{n}(\mathbb{R}), and SpUn⁡(ℂ)\SpU_{n}(\mathbb{C}). Let kk be an arbitrary field of characteristic zero.

Theorem 6.1 (The density theorem).

With the above notation, we have:

  1. (a)

    CC is a Zariski-dense subgroup of G⁡(ℂ)\GG(\mathbb{C}); and

  2. (b)

    G⁡(ℚ)\GG(\mathbb{Q}) is a Zariski-dense subgroup of G⁡(k)\GG(k).

Proof.

For (a), see the proof of [Kr, Anhang II, Satz 4]. We give a more elementary proof for GL\GL and SL\SL in Appendix A, see A.5 and A.6. We also prove (b) in Appendix A, see Theorem A.7. ∎

By k⁡[Z]k[Z], we will mean one of k⁡[Y]k[Y] or k⁡[X,Y]k[X,Y]. In either case, we have a rational action of G⁡(k)\GG(k) on k⁡[Z]k[Z], as described in Section 3. Note that CC is a compact Lie group, and the action of G⁡(ℂ)\GG(\mathbb{C}) on ℂ⁡[Z]\mathbb{C}[Z] restricts to a smooth action of CC. We have the following group extensions.

We will first show how the computation of the Reynolds operator for G⁡(k)\GG(k) reduces to that for CC. The key point is that the action is rational, and each inclusion above is Zariski-dense by Theorem 6.1. This reduction is useful because CC is a compact Lie group; thus, we have its Reynolds operator by Theorem 5.6.

Proposition 6.2.

Let f1,…,fn∈ℚ​[Z]G⁡(ℚ)f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}\in\mathbb{Q}[Z]^{\GG(\mathbb{Q})} be generating invariants, that is, we have ℚ​[Z]G⁡(ℚ)=ℚ⁡[f1,…,fn]\mathbb{Q}[Z]^{\GG(\mathbb{Q})}=\mathbb{Q}[f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}]. Then, the equality k​[Z]G⁡(k)=k⁡[f1,…,fn]k[Z]^{\GG(k)}=k[f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}] holds. In particular, we have the inclusion ℚ​[Z]G⁡(ℚ)⊆k​[Z]G⁡(k)\mathbb{Q}[Z]^{\GG(\mathbb{Q})}\subseteq k[Z]^{\GG(k)} as subsets of k⁡[Z]k[Z].

Proof.

We first show that each fif_{i} is G⁡(k)\GG(k)-invariant. To this end, note that the equation

σ⁡(fi)−fi=0\sigma(f_{i})-f_{i}=0

holds for each fixed ii and for all σ∈G⁡(ℚ)\sigma\in\GG(\mathbb{Q}). Because the action is rational and G⁡(ℚ)\GG(\mathbb{Q}) is Zariski-dense in G⁡(k)\GG(k) by Theorem A.7, the above equation must hold for all σ∈G⁡(k)\sigma\in\GG(k). In other words, each fif_{i} is G⁡(k)\GG(k)-invariant.

We now prove the inclusion k​[Z]G⁡(k)⊆k⁡[f1,…,fn]k[Z]^{\GG(k)}\subseteq k[f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}]. Let BB be a ℚ\mathbb{Q}-basis for kk. Given h∈k​[Z]G⁡(k)h\in k[Z]^{\GG(k)}, write

h=∑b∈Bb​hbh=\sum_{b\in B}bh_{b}

for hb∈ℚ⁡[Z]h_{b}\in\mathbb{Q}[Z]. If we apply σ∈G⁡(ℚ)\sigma\in\GG(\mathbb{Q}) to the above equation, we get

h=∑b∈Bb​σ​(hb)h=\sum_{b\in B}b\sigma(h_{b})

because σ⁡(h)=h\sigma(h)=h and σ⁡(b)=b\sigma(b)=b for all b∈kb\in k. Comparing the two displayed equations above gives us that each hbh_{b} is fixed by G⁡(ℚ)\GG(\mathbb{Q}) and thus hb∈ℚ⁡[f1,…,fn]h_{b}\in\mathbb{Q}[f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}] for all bb. In turn, h∈k⁡[f1,…,fn]h\in k[f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}], as desired. ∎

Proposition 6.3.

Let ℛk:k⁡[Z]-↠k​[Z]G⁡(k)\mathcal{R}_{k}\colon k[Z]\relbar\joinrel\twoheadrightarrow k[Z]^{\GG(k)} denote the Reynolds operator over the field kk. The following diagram commutes

In particular, if μ∈k⁡[Z]\mu\in k[Z] is a monomial, then

(6.1) ℛk​(μ)=ℛℂ​(μ).\mathcal{R}_{k}(\mu)=\mathcal{R}_{\mathbb{C}}(\mu).

The above equation makes sense by interpreting μ\mu as an element of ℂ⁡[Z]\mathbb{C}[Z].

Proof.

In view of Proposition 6.2, we may extend ℛℚ\mathcal{R}_{\mathbb{Q}} kk-linearly to obtain a retraction π\pi making the diagram

commute. We need to show that π=ℛk\pi=\mathcal{R}_{k}. By the uniqueness of the Reynolds operator, Theorem 4.2, it suffices to show that π\pi is G⁡(k)\GG(k)-equivariant. Note that G⁡(k)\GG(k)-equivariance can be checked on monomials, where it is true again by the Zariski-density of G⁡(ℚ)\GG(\mathbb{Q}). This proves that the diagram commutes. Now, if μ∈ℚ⁡[Y]\mu\in\mathbb{Q}[Y] is a monomial, then the diagram gives us ℛk​(μ)=ℛℚ​(μ)\mathcal{R}_{k}(\mu)=\mathcal{R}_{\mathbb{Q}}(\mu). Because kk was arbitrary, we get Equation 6.1. ∎

The Zariski-density of CC in G⁡(ℂ)\GG(\mathbb{C}) similarly yields the following proposition.

Proposition 6.4.

The equality ℂ​[Z]G⁡(ℂ)=ℂ​[Z]C\mathbb{C}[Z]^{\GG(\mathbb{C})}=\mathbb{C}[Z]^{C} holds, and the splitting ℛ:ℂ⁡[Z]-→ℂ​[Z]C\mathcal{R}\colon\mathbb{C}[Z]\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}[Z]^{C} described in Theorem 5.6 is G⁡(ℂ)\GG(\mathbb{C})-equivariant. In other words, ℛ\mathcal{R} is the Reynolds operator for the G⁡(ℂ)\GG(\mathbb{C})-action, by Theorem 4.2.

Remark 6.5.

The above has now made the computation of ℛk\mathcal{R}_{k} clear: because the Reynolds operator ℛk\mathcal{R}_{k} is a kk-linear map, it suffices to compute it on monomials; and for monomials, ℛk\mathcal{R}_{k} agrees with the Reynolds operator for the Lie group CC by Equation 6.1 and Proposition 6.4.

In the following two subsections, we describe algorithms to implement this splitting on a computer algebra system.

6.3. Some remarks

We stress that the only non-algebraic calculations above are the integrals of monomial functions over CC, where CC is one of Ut⁡(ℂ)\UU_{t}(\mathbb{C}), SUt⁡(ℂ)\SU_{t}(\mathbb{C}), Ot⁡(ℝ)\OO_{t}(\mathbb{R}), or SpUt⁡(ℂ)\SpU_{t}(\mathbb{C}). Note moreover that these are scalar functions. While we discussed the theory of integration of vector-valued functions to prove the above, one only needs to work with ℂ\mathbb{C}-valued functions in practice.

The integration of these monomial functions over Ut⁡(ℂ)\UU_{t}(\mathbb{C}), Ot⁡(ℝ)\OO_{t}(\mathbb{R}), and SpUt⁡(ℂ)\SpU_{t}(\mathbb{C}) is of interest in various fields of mathematical physics, see the introduction of [GL]. Methods to compute these integrals are described in [CŚ, GL]. In particular, the integration of arbitrary monomial functions over Ut⁡(ℂ)\UU_{t}(\mathbb{C}) has been implemented in the Mathematica package IntU [PM]. Using this package, we have implemented the splitting Equation 6.3 for the action (R2) of GLt⁡(ℂ)\GL_{t}(\mathbb{C}) in the computer algebra system SageMath [Th]. We have also implemented the splitting Equation 6.2 for the action (R1) of SL2⁡(ℂ)\SL_{2}(\mathbb{C}) using Theorem 7.5.

For SLt⁡(k)\SL_{t}(k) and Ot⁡(k)\OO_{t}(k), the method described in Section 6.2 for the action (R2) may be modified as follows.

  1. (a)

    (Special linear group) If C=SLt⁡(ℂ)∩Ut⁡(ℂ)C=\SL_{t}(\mathbb{C})\cap\UU_{t}(\mathbb{C}), then the inverse of U∈CU\in C is given by the adjugate adj⁡(U)\adj(U). Note that the entries of adj⁡(U)\adj(U) are polynomials in the entries of UU, so we may modify ϕ\phi as

    ϕ:k⁡[X,Y]\displaystyle\phi\colon k[X,Y] -→k[X,Y][U]\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow k[X,Y][U]
    X\displaystyle X ⟼X​adj⁡(U),\displaystyle\longmapsto X\adj(U),
    Y\displaystyle Y ⟼U​Y.\displaystyle\longmapsto UY.
  2. (b)

    (Orthogonal group) If C=Ot⁡(ℂ)∩Ut⁡(ℂ)C=\OO_{t}(\mathbb{C})\cap\UU_{t}(\mathbb{C}), then the inverse of U∈CU\in C is just the transpose UtrU^{\operatorname{tr}}, so we may modify ϕ\phi as

    ϕ:k⁡[X,Y]\displaystyle\phi\colon k[X,Y] -→k[X,Y][U]\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow k[X,Y][U]
    X\displaystyle X ⟼X​Utr,\displaystyle\longmapsto XU^{\operatorname{tr}},
    Y\displaystyle Y ⟼U​Y.\displaystyle\longmapsto UY.

7. Explicit formulae

In this section, we use the formulae of Section 6 to compute the Reynolds operators for SL2\SL_{2} and GLt\GL_{t}. We give expressions for these in terms of the invariants described in Theorem 3.1.

7.1. The Reynolds operator for SL2\SL_{2}

We use formula Equation 6.2 to compute the Reynolds operator ℛ\mathcal{R} for the standard action (R1) of SL2⁡(k)\SL_{2}(k) on k⁡[Y2×N]k[Y_{2\times N}]; the relevant monomial integrals are determined in Theorem 7.5 and we can thus compute ℛ\mathcal{R} on any element of k⁡[Y]k[Y]. We begin the section by recording the value of ℛ\mathcal{R} on various families of monomials, postponing the proofs until the end of the section. By Theorem 3.1, we know that k​[Y]SL2⁡(k)k[Y]^{\SL_{2}(k)} is generated by the size 22 minors of YY. For ease of notation, we write

Y=[a1a2⋯aNb1b2⋯bN],{Δ}≔{size 2 minors of Y},andΔi,j≔aibj−ajbi.Y=\begin{bmatrix}a_{1}&a_{2}&\cdots&a_{N}\\ b_{1}&b_{2}&\cdots&b_{N}\\ \end{bmatrix},\qquad\{\Delta\}\coloneqq\{\text{size $2$ minors of $Y$}\},\qquad\text{and}\qquad\Delta_{i,j}\coloneqq a_{i}b_{j}-a_{j}b_{i}.

The next theorem describes the Reynolds operator on k⁡[Y2×2]k[Y_{2\times 2}].

Theorem 7.1.

Let ℛ:k⁡[Y2×2]-→k⁡[{Δ}]\mathcal{R}\colon k[Y_{2\times 2}]\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow k[\{\Delta\}] be the Reynolds operator and μ∈k⁡[Y2×2]\mu\in k[Y_{2\times 2}] a monomial.

  1. (a)

    If μ\mu is of the form (a1​b2)n​(a2​b1)m(a_{1}b_{2})^{n}(a_{2}b_{1})^{m} for some nonnegative integers nn and mm, then

    (7.1) ℛ⁡(μ)=ℛ⁡((a1​b2)n​(a2​b1)m)=n!​m!(n+m+1)!​Δ1,2n​Δ2,1m;\mathcal{R}(\mu)=\mathcal{R}\left((a_{1}b_{2})^{n}(a_{2}b_{1})^{m}\right)=\frac{n!m!}{(n+m+1)!}\Delta_{1,2}^{n}\Delta_{2,1}^{m};

    in particular, for n⩾0n\geqslant 0, we have

    (7.2) ℛ⁡((a1​b2)n)=1n+1​Δ1,2n.\mathcal{R}\left((a_{1}b_{2})^{n}\right)=\frac{1}{n+1}\Delta_{1,2}^{n}.
  2. (b)

    If μ\mu is not of the above form, then

    ℛ⁡(μ)=0.\mathcal{R}(\mu)=0.

We give k⁡[Y2×N]k[Y_{2\times N}] a multi-grading by defining deg⁡(ai)=(1,0)\deg(a_{i})=(1,0) and deg⁡(bi)=(0,1)\deg(b_{i})=(0,1) for all 1⩽i⩽N1\leqslant i\leqslant N.

Theorem 7.2.

Let μ∈k⁡[Y]\mu\in k[Y] be a monomial such that deg⁡(μ)=(m,n)\deg(\mu)=(m,n) with m≠nm\neq n. Then, ℛ⁡(μ)=0\mathcal{R}(\mu)=0.

Computations suggest that Equation 7.1 generalises as follows.

Conjecture 7.3.

For all nonnegative integers ii, jj, kk, we have

ℛ⁡((a1​b2)i​(a1​b3)j​(a2​b3)k)=(i+j)!​(k+j)!(i+j+k+1)!​j!​Δ1,2i​Δ1,3j​Δ2,3k.\mathcal{R}\left((a_{1}b_{2})^{i}(a_{1}b_{3})^{j}(a_{2}b_{3})^{k}\right)=\frac{(i+j)!(k+j)!}{(i+j+k+1)!j!}\Delta_{1,2}^{i}\Delta_{1,3}^{j}\Delta_{2,3}^{k}.
Conjecture 7.4.

For all nonnegative integers nn, we have

ℛ⁡((a1​a2​a3​b1​b2​b3)2​n+1)=0.\mathcal{R}\left((a_{1}a_{2}a_{3}b_{1}b_{2}b_{3})^{2n+1}\right)=0.
Theorem 7.5.

For all nonnegative integers aa, bb, cc, dd, we have

∫SU2⁡(ℂ)u11a​u12b​u21c​u22d={(−1)b​a!​b!(a+b+1)!if a=d and b=c,0else.\int_{\SU_{2}(\mathbb{C})}u_{11}^{a}u_{12}^{b}u_{21}^{c}u_{22}^{d}=\begin{cases}(-1)^{b}\dfrac{a!b!}{(a+b+1)!}&\text{if $a=d$ and $b=c$},\\[3.0pt] 0&\text{else}.\end{cases}
Proof.

See Identity B.5. ∎

We say that a monomial in k⁡[Y]k[Y] is balanced if it is a product of monomials of the form ai​bja_{i}b_{j} with i≠ji\neq j, and unbalanced otherwise. The following are straightforward observations.

  1. (a)

    The algebra of minors k⁡[{Δ}]k[\{\Delta\}] sits inside the kk-subalgebra generated by the balanced monomials.

  2. (b)

    If μ∈k⁡[Y]\mu\in k[Y] is a balanced monomial, then deg⁡(μ)=(d,d)\deg(\mu)=(d,d) for some d⩾0d\geqslant 0.

Note however that deg⁡(a1​b1)=(1,1)\deg(a_{1}b_{1})=(1,1), yet a1​b1a_{1}b_{1} is unbalanced.

Remark 7.6.

Assuming Conjecture 7.3, the k⁡[{Δ}]k[\{\Delta\}]-linearity of ℛ\mathcal{R} would then determine the value of ℛ\mathcal{R} on any balanced monomial in k⁡[Y2×3]k[Y_{2\times 3}]. For example, one may verify Conjecture 7.3 in the two cases needed for the following computation and obtain

ℛ⁡((a1​b2)​(a2​b3)​(a3​b1))=ℛ⁡((a1​b2)​(a2​b3)​(a1​b3−Δ1,3))=(16−16)​Δ1,2​Δ1,3​Δ2,3=0.\mathcal{R}\left((a_{1}b_{2})(a_{2}b_{3})(a_{3}b_{1})\right)=\mathcal{R}\left((a_{1}b_{2})(a_{2}b_{3})(a_{1}b_{3}-\Delta_{1,3})\right)=\left(\frac{1}{6}-\frac{1}{6}\right)\Delta_{1,2}\Delta_{1,3}\Delta_{2,3}=0.

The above gives us the case n=0n=0 in Conjecture 7.4. In particular, it shows that a balanced monomial may be in the kernel of ℛ\mathcal{R}; Theorem 7.1 tells us that this does not happen for k⁡[Y2×2]k[Y_{2\times 2}], where the monomials in the kernel are precisely the unbalanced ones.

Remark 7.7.

It is not true that the image of a monomial is again a monomial in the Δi,j\Delta_{i,j}. One checks that

ℛ⁡(a1​b2​a3​b4)=13​Δ1,2​Δ3,4−16​Δ1,3​Δ2,4.\mathcal{R}(a_{1}b_{2}a_{3}b_{4})=\frac{1}{3}\Delta_{1,2}\Delta_{3,4}-\frac{1}{6}\Delta_{1,3}\Delta_{2,4}.

The expression on the right is not divisible by any Δi,j\Delta_{i,j} and thus cannot be expressed as a monomial in the {Δ}\{\Delta\}.

Proof of Theorem 7.2.

Consider the element σ=(2002−1)∈SL2⁡(k)\sigma=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&0\\ 0&2^{-1}\\ \end{smallmatrix}\right)\in\SL_{2}(k). Proof of Theorem 7.1 (b).

7.2. The Reynolds operator for GLt\GL_{t}

Let tt, nn, mm be positive integers, and ℛ:k⁡[Xm×t,Yt×n]-→k​[X,Y]GLt⁡(k)\mathcal{R}\colon k[X_{m\times t},Y_{t\times n}]\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow k[X,Y]^{\GL_{t}(k)} the Reynolds operator for the action (R2). By Theorem 3.1, we know the image of ℛ\mathcal{R} to lie in k⁡[X​Y]k[XY], the subalgebra of k⁡[X,Y]k[X,Y] generated by the entries of X​YXY. Experimenting with the package IntU [PM] suggests a formula similar to Equation 7.2.

8. Comparison with positive characteristic

The classical groups GL\GL, SL\SL, O\OO, Sp\Sp are typically not linearly reductive in positive characteristic. Thus, there is no guarantee of the existence of splittings that are linear over the fixed subring. In fact, the following theorem tells us that this is essentially never the case.

Theorem 8.1 ([HJPS, Theorem 1.1]).

Let kk be a field of characteristic p>0p>0. Fix positive integers mm, nn, and tt, and let R⊆SR\subseteq S denote one of the following inclusions:

  1. (a)

    k⁡[X​Y]⊆k⁡[Xm×t,Yt×n]k[XY]\subseteq k[X_{m\times t},Y_{t\times n}];

  2. (b)

    k⁡[{Δ}]⊆k⁡[Yt×n]k[\{\Delta\}]\subseteq k[Y_{t\times n}] with t⩽nt\leqslant n, where {Δ}\{\Delta\} is the set of size tt minors of YY;

  3. (c)

    k⁡[Ytr​Y]⊆k⁡[Yt×n]k[Y^{\operatorname{tr}}Y]\subseteq k[Y_{t\times n}];

  4. (d)

    k⁡[Ytr​Ω​Y]⊆k⁡[Y2​t×n]k[Y^{\operatorname{tr}}\Omega Y]\subseteq k[Y_{2t\times n}].

Then the inclusion R⊆SR\subseteq S splits RR-linearly if and only if, in the respective cases,

  1. (a)

    t=1t=1 or min⁡{m,n}⩽t\min\{m,n\}\leqslant t;

  2. (b)

    t=1t=1 or t=nt=n;

  3. (c)

    t=1t=1; t=2t=2 and pp is odd; p=2p=2 and n⩽(t+1)/2n\leqslant(t+1)/2; or pp is odd and n⩽(t+2)/2n\leqslant(t+2)/2;

  4. (d)

    n⩽t+1n\leqslant t+1.

Remark 8.2.

The above theorem does not reference any group (action). However, compare with Theorem 3.1 to see the connection for infinite fields of positive characteristic.

Remark 8.3.

We describe a curious implication of Theorem 8.1. We revisit formula Equation 7.2:

ℛ⁡((a1​b2)n)=1n+1​Δ1,2n.\mathcal{R}\left((a_{1}b_{2})^{n}\right)=\frac{1}{n+1}\Delta_{1,2}^{n}.

Note the denominator ‘n+1n+1’. This means that each prime number shows up as a factor of the denominator for some monomial. Said differently, ℛ\mathcal{R} does not restrict to a map ℤ(p)​[Y]-→ℤ(p)​[{Δ}]\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}[Y]\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}[\{\Delta\}] for any prime p>0p>0, where ℤ(p)\mathbb{Z}_{(p)} is the subring of ℚ\mathbb{Q} defined as

ℤ(p)≔{ab∈ℚ:a,b∈ℤwithp∤b}.\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}\coloneqq\left\{\frac{a}{b}\in\mathbb{Q}:a,b\in\mathbb{Z}\ \text{with}\ p\nmid b\right\}.

Theorem 8.1 tells us that this must essentially always happen for any of the Reynolds operators described in the paper. More generally, the above must happen for essentially any splitting that is linear over the subring.

Indeed, pick a situation in Theorem 8.1 where the inclusion does not split in positive characteristic. For example, 𝔽p​[{Δ}]​⸦-→𝔽p​[Yt×n]\mathbb{F}_{p}[\{\Delta\}]\lhook\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_{p}[Y_{t\times n}] with 1<t<n1<t<n. As discussed earlier, the inclusion ℚ⁡[{Δ}]​⸦-→ℚ⁡[Yt×n]\mathbb{Q}[\{\Delta\}]\lhook\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow\mathbb{Q}[Y_{t\times n}] does split. Moreover, if we are only interested in splittings that are linear over the subring, then there are typically more than one. Let π:ℚ⁡[Yt×n]-→ℚ⁡[{Δ}]\pi\colon\mathbb{Q}[Y_{t\times n}]\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow\mathbb{Q}[\{\Delta\}] be any such ℚ⁡[{Δ}]\mathbb{Q}[\{\Delta\}]-linear splitting. The following must hold: given any prime p>0p>0, there exists some monomial μ=μ⁡(p)∈ℚ⁡[Y]\mu=\mu(p)\in\mathbb{Q}[Y] such that when we express π⁡(μ)\pi(\mu) as a polynomial in the {Δ}\{\Delta\} with rational coefficients, then one of the coefficients has denominator divisible by pp. Indeed, if this were not the case for some prime pp, then π\pi would restrict to a splitting ℤ(p)​[Y]-→ℤ(p)​[{Δ}]\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}[Y]\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}[\{\Delta\}], and we could go mod pp to obtain an 𝔽p​[{Δ}]\mathbb{F}_{p}[\{\Delta\}]-linear splitting, contradicting Theorem 8.1.

Appendix A Proof of the density theorem

Definition A.1.

For XX a topological space and YY a subspace of XX, a retraction of XX onto YY is a continuous function r:X-→Yr\colon X\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow Y satisfying r⁡(y)=yr(y)=y for all y∈Y⊆Xy\in Y\subseteq X.

Lemma A.2.

Let kk be a field, and S⊆kS\subseteq k be an infinite subset. If f∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]f\in k[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] is a polynomial vanishing on the product Sn⊆𝔸knS^{n}\subseteq\mathbb{A}_{k}^{n}, then ff is the zero polynomial. Equivalently, SnS^{n} is Zariski-dense in 𝔸kn\mathbb{A}_{k}^{n}.

Proof.

We prove the statement by induction on nn. It is clear for n=1n=1. Assume n>1n>1 and suppose ff is nonzero. Write f=f0+f1​xn+⋯+fd​xndf=f_{0}+f_{1}x_{n}+\cdots+f_{d}x_{n}^{d} with d⩾0d\geqslant 0, fd≠0f_{d}\neq 0, and fi∈k⁡[x1,…,xn−1]f_{i}\in k[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n-1}]. By induction, there exists 𝐬=(s1,…,sn−1)∈Sn−1\mathbf{s}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{n-1})\in S^{n-1} with fd​(𝐬)≠0f_{d}(\mathbf{s})\neq 0. Then, f⁡(𝐬,xn)f(\mathbf{s},x_{n}) is a nonzero polynomial in one variable, and this finishes the proof. ∎

Lemma A.3.

Let XX be a topological space, Z⊆XZ\subseteq X a dense subspace, and Y⊆XY\subseteq X a subspace such that there exists a retraction r:X-↠Yr\colon X\relbar\joinrel\twoheadrightarrow Y with r⁡(Z)⊆Zr(Z)\subseteq Z. Then, Z∩YZ\cap Y is dense in YY.

Proof.

Let y∈Yy\in Y be arbitrary. As ZZ is dense in XX, there exists a net ⟨zλ⟩λ∈Λ\langle z_{\lambda}\rangle_{\lambda\in\Lambda} in ZZ with zλ-→yz_{\lambda}\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow y. In turn, ⟨r⁡(zλ)⟩λ\langle r(z_{\lambda})\rangle_{\lambda} is a net in Z∩YZ\cap Y converging to yy. ∎

For the next few proofs, we define the function

(A.1) r:GLn⁡(k)\displaystyle r\colon\GL_{n}(k) -→SLn(k)\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow\SL_{n}(k)
U=[u11u12⋯u1​nu21u22⋯u2​n⋱un​1un​2⋯un​n]\displaystyle U=\begin{bmatrix}u_{11}&u_{12}&\cdots&u_{1n}\\ u_{21}&u_{22}&\cdots&u_{2n}\\ \vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ u_{n1}&u_{n2}&\cdots&u_{nn}\end{bmatrix} ⟼[u11detUu12detU⋯u1​ndetUu21u22⋯u2​n⋱un​1un​2⋯un​n].\displaystyle\longmapsto\begin{bmatrix}\frac{u_{11}}{\det U}&\frac{u_{12}}{\det U}&\cdots&\frac{u_{1n}}{\det U}\\ u_{21}&u_{22}&\cdots&u_{2n}\\ \vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ u_{n1}&u_{n2}&\cdots&u_{nn}\end{bmatrix}.

That is, rr scales the first row of UU by 1detU\frac{1}{\det U}.

Lemma A.4.

For any field kk, the function rr defined by Equation A.1 is a retraction of GLn⁡(k)\GL_{n}(k) onto SLn⁡(k)\SL_{n}(k).

Proof.

The multilinearity of det\det implies that det(r⁡(U))=1\det(r(U))=1 for all U∈GLn⁡(ℂ)U\in\GL_{n}(\mathbb{C}), that is, rr indeed takes values in SLn⁡(k)\SL_{n}(k). The function rr is continuous in the Zariski topology because it is given by rational functions. It is clear that the restriction of rr to SLn⁡(k)\SL_{n}(k) is the identity. ∎

Proposition A.5.

For all n⩾1n\geqslant 1, the subgroup Un⁡(ℂ)\UU_{n}(\mathbb{C}) is Zariski-dense in GLn⁡(ℂ)\GL_{n}(\mathbb{C}).

Proof.

Let CC be the Zariski closure of Un⁡(ℂ)\UU_{n}(\mathbb{C}) in GLn⁡(ℂ)\GL_{n}(\mathbb{C}). Write C=V⁡(𝔞)∩GLn⁡(ℂ)C=V(\mathfrak{a})\cap\GL_{n}(\mathbb{C}) for 𝔞\mathfrak{a} an ideal. Let f∈𝔞f\in\mathfrak{a}. Note that if z1,…,znz_{1},\ldots,z_{n} are elements of the unit circle 𝕊1\mathbb{S}^{1}, then diag⁡(z1,…,zn)\diag(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}) is an element of Un\UU_{n}. Thus, ff vanishes on all diagonal matrices with entries coming from 𝕊1\mathbb{S}^{1}. By Lemma A.2, we see that ff must vanish on all diagonal matrices. Thus, CC contains all invertible diagonal matrices.

Because GLn⁡(ℂ)\GL_{n}(\mathbb{C}) is a topological group in the Zariski topology, and Un⁡(ℂ)\UU_{n}(\mathbb{C}) is a subgroup, it follows that CC is a subgroup. As every invertible matrix can be decomposed as U​D​VUDV with U,V∈Un⁡(ℂ)U,V\in\UU_{n}(\mathbb{C}) and DD invertible diagonal, we are done. ∎

Proposition A.6.

For all n⩾1n\geqslant 1, the subgroup SUn⁡(ℂ)\SU_{n}(\mathbb{C}) is Zariski-dense in SLn⁡(ℂ)\SL_{n}(\mathbb{C}).

Proof.

We use Lemma A.3 with X=GLn⁡(ℂ)X=\GL_{n}(\mathbb{C}), Z=Un⁡(ℂ)Z=\UU_{n}(\mathbb{C}), Y=SLn⁡(ℂ)Y=\SL_{n}(\mathbb{C}), and rr given by Equation A.1. The density of ZZ then follows from Proposition A.5. All that is left to be shown is that r⁡(Un⁡(ℂ))⊆Un⁡(ℂ)r(\UU_{n}(\mathbb{C}))\subseteq\UU_{n}(\mathbb{C}). To this end, note that a matrix is unitary if and only if its rows form an orthonormal basis. If U∈Un⁡(ℂ)U\in\UU_{n}(\mathbb{C}), then det(U)∈𝕊1\det(U)\in\mathbb{S}^{1} and thus, the rows of r⁡(U)r(U) continue to be orthonormal. ∎

Theorem A.7.

Let kk be a field of characteristic zero. For each of the following inclusions, the subgroup is Zariski-dense in the larger group.

  1. (a)

    GLn⁡(ℚ)⊆GLn⁡(k)\GL_{n}(\mathbb{Q})\subseteq\GL_{n}(k),

  2. (b)

    SLn⁡(ℚ)⊆SLn⁡(k)\SL_{n}(\mathbb{Q})\subseteq\SL_{n}(k),

  3. (c)

    On⁡(ℚ)⊆On⁡(k)\OO_{n}(\mathbb{Q})\subseteq\OO_{n}(k), and

  4. (d)

    Sp2​n⁡(ℚ)⊆Sp2​n⁡(k)\Sp_{2n}(\mathbb{Q})\subseteq\Sp_{2n}(k).

Proof.

General linear group: By Lemma A.2, the subspace ℚn2\mathbb{Q}^{n^{2}} is dense in 𝔸kn2\mathbb{A}_{k}^{n^{2}}. Intersecting with the open set GLn⁡(k)\GL_{n}(k) gives us (a).

Special linear group: (b) then follows by use of Lemma A.3 with X=GLn⁡(k)X=\GL_{n}(k), Y=SLn⁡(k)Y=\SL_{n}(k), Z=GLn⁡(ℚ)Z=\GL_{n}(\mathbb{Q}), and rr given by Equation A.1.

Orthogonal group: We note that the orthogonal group On⁡(k)\OO_{n}(k) is generated by the set of reflections

R⁡(k)≔{I−2​u​utrutr​u:u∈kn with utr​u≠0},R(k)\coloneqq\left\{I-\frac{2uu^{\operatorname{tr}}}{u^{\operatorname{tr}}u}:\text{$u\in k^{n}$ with $u^{\operatorname{tr}}u\neq 0$}\right\},

in fact the Cartan–Dieudonné theorem states that every orthogonal matrix is a product of at most nn such reflections, see [Di, Sc]. Because the closure of On⁡(ℚ)\OO_{n}(\mathbb{Q}) must be a subgroup of On⁡(k)\OO_{n}(k), it suffices to show that R⁡(ℚ)R(\mathbb{Q}) is dense in R⁡(k)R(k). To this end, note that I⁡(k)≔{u∈kn:utr​u≠0}I(k)\coloneqq\{u\in k^{n}\colon u^{\operatorname{tr}}u\neq 0\} is an open subset of 𝔸kn\mathbb{A}_{k}^{n} and thus intersecting with the dense set ℚn\mathbb{Q}^{n}, we get that I⁡(ℚ)I(\mathbb{Q}) is dense in I⁡(k)I(k). Now, R⁡(k)R(k) is the image of I⁡(k)I(k) under the continuous map u⟼I−2​u​utrutr​uu\longmapsto I-\frac{2uu^{\operatorname{tr}}}{u^{\operatorname{tr}}u} and hence R⁡(ℚ)R(\mathbb{Q}) is dense in R⁡(k)R(k).

Symplectic group: (d) follows similarly by using the fact that the symplectic group Sp2​n⁡(k)\Sp_{2n}(k) is generated by

[AOO(Atr)−1],[IBOI],and[OI−IO],\begin{bmatrix}A&O\\ O&(A^{\operatorname{tr}})^{-1}\\ \end{bmatrix},\qquad\begin{bmatrix}I&B\\ O&I\\ \end{bmatrix},\quad\text{and}\quad\begin{bmatrix}O&I\\ -I&O\\ \end{bmatrix},

where AA varies over SLn⁡(k)\SL_{n}(k), and BB over all symmetric n×nn\times n matrices. This description is originally due to \CiteauthorDieudonneGenerators [Dia] and can also be found in [OM, §2.2]. ∎

Appendix B Multinomial coefficient and integration identities

Identity B.1.

For integers a,b⩾0a,b\geqslant 0, we have

∫01ta​(1−t)b​𝑑t=a!​b!(a+b+1)!.\int_{0}^{1}t^{a}(1-t)^{b}\,{\mathrm{d}}t=\frac{a!b!}{(a+b+1)!}.
Proof.

The formula is readily verified if b=0b=0. For a⩾0a\geqslant 0 and b>0b>0, integration by parts yields

∫01ta​(1−t)b​𝑑t=ba+1​∫01ta+1​(1−t)b−1​𝑑t.\int_{0}^{1}t^{a}(1-t)^{b}\,{\mathrm{d}}t=\frac{b}{a+1}\int_{0}^{1}t^{a+1}(1-t)^{b-1}\,{\mathrm{d}}t.

Repeated application of the above gives the desired formula. ∎

Identity B.2.

Let n⩾0n\geqslant 0 be an integer. One has the identity

(x+y)nn+1=∑2​i+j+k=n(ni,i,j,k)​(i+j)!​(i+k)!(n+1)!​xi+j​yi+k,\frac{(x+y)^{n}}{n+1}=\sum_{2i+j+k=n}\binom{n}{i,i,j,k}\frac{(i+j)!(i+k)!}{(n+1)!}x^{i+j}y^{i+k},

where, explicitly, the sum is taken over all triples (i,j,k)∈ℕ3(i,j,k)\in\mathbb{N}^{3} satisfying 2​i+j+k=n2i+j+k=n.

Proof.

Note that

(ni,i,j,k)​(i+j)!​(i+k)!(n+1)!=n!i!​i!​j!​k!​(i+j)!​(i+k)!(n+1)!=1n+1​(i+ji)​(i+kk).\binom{n}{i,i,j,k}\frac{(i+j)!(i+k)!}{(n+1)!}=\frac{n!}{i!i!j!k!}\frac{(i+j)!(i+k)!}{(n+1)!}=\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{i+j}{i}\binom{i+k}{k}.

Thus, the identity of interest is equivalent to

(x+y)n=∑2​i+j+k=n(i+ji)​(i+kk)​xi+j​yi+k.(x+y)^{n}=\sum_{2i+j+k=n}\binom{i+j}{i}\binom{i+k}{k}x^{i+j}y^{i+k}.

Because both sides of the equation are homogeneous of degree nn, it suffices to verify that

(⋆\star) (x+1)n=∑2​i+j+k=n(i+ji)​(i+kk)​xi+j.\displaystyle(x+1)^{n}=\sum_{2i+j+k=n}\binom{i+j}{i}\binom{i+k}{k}x^{i+j}.

To prove the above identity, we need to show that the coefficient of xax^{a} is the same on both sides for each 0⩽a⩽n0\leqslant a\leqslant n. The coefficient of xax^{a} on the right-hand-side of Equation  ⋆ is given by

∑2​i+j+k=ni+j=a(i+ji)​(i+kk)=∑i+k=n−a(ai)​(i+ki)=∑i(ai)​(n−ai).\displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}2i+j+k=n\\ i+j=a\end{subarray}}\binom{i+j}{i}\binom{i+k}{k}=\sum_{i+k=n-a}\binom{a}{i}\binom{i+k}{i}=\sum_{i}\binom{a}{i}\binom{n-a}{i}.

Thus, it suffices to prove that

(†\dagger) (na)=∑i(ai)​(n−ai).\displaystyle\binom{n}{a}=\sum_{i}\binom{a}{i}\binom{n-a}{i}.

To this end, note that

(1+X)a​(1+Y)n−a=∑i,j(ai)​(n−aj)​Xi​Yj.(1+X)^{a}(1+Y)^{n-a}=\sum_{i,j}\binom{a}{i}\binom{n-a}{j}X^{i}Y^{j}.

Substituting Y=1/XY=1/X gives

(1+X)a​(1+1X)n−a=∑i,j(ai)​(n−aj)​Xi−j.(1+X)^{a}\left(1+\frac{1}{X}\right)^{n-a}=\sum_{i,j}\binom{a}{i}\binom{n-a}{j}X^{i-j}.

Thus,

1Xn−a​(1+X)n=∑i,j(ai)​(n−aj)​Xi−j.\frac{1}{X^{n-a}}(1+X)^{n}=\sum_{i,j}\binom{a}{i}\binom{n-a}{j}X^{i-j}.

Comparing the coefficient of X0X^{0} on both sides gives us Equation  † . ∎

Identity B.3.

For integers m,n⩾0m,n\geqslant 0, one has the identity

∑k=0n(nk)​(−1)km+k+1=m!​n!(m+n+1)!.\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}\frac{(-1)^{k}}{m+k+1}=\frac{m!n!}{(m+n+1)!}.
Proof.

We note

∑k=0n(nk)​(−1)km+k+1\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}\frac{(-1)^{k}}{m+k+1} =∑k=0n(nk)​(−1)k​∫01tm+k​𝑑t\displaystyle=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}(-1)^{k}\int_{0}^{1}t^{m+k}\,{\mathrm{d}}t
=∫01tm⋅∑k=0n(nk)​(−t)k​𝑑t\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{1}t^{m}\cdot\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}(-t)^{k}\,{\mathrm{d}}t
=∫01tm​(1−t)n​𝑑t\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{1}t^{m}(1-t)^{n}\,{\mathrm{d}}t
=m!​n!(m+n+1)!,\displaystyle=\frac{m!n!}{(m+n+1)!},

where the last step uses Identity B.1. ∎

Identity B.4.

For integers a,b⩾0a,b\geqslant 0, we have

∫0π/2cos2​a⁡(θ)​sin2​b⁡(θ)​sin⁡(2​θ)​𝑑θ=a!​b!(a+b+1)!.\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\cos^{2a}(\theta)\sin^{2b}(\theta)\sin(2\theta)\,{\mathrm{d}}\theta=\frac{a!b!}{(a+b+1)!}.
Proof.

The integrand can be rewritten as

cos2​a⁡(θ)​sin2​b⁡(θ)​sin⁡(2​θ)\displaystyle\cos^{2a}(\theta)\sin^{2b}(\theta)\sin(2\theta) =2​cos2​a+1⁡(θ)​sin2​b+1⁡(θ)\displaystyle=2\cos^{2a+1}(\theta)\sin^{2b+1}(\theta)
=2​(cos2⁡(θ))a​(sin⁡(θ))2​b+1​cos⁡(θ)\displaystyle=2(\cos^{2}(\theta))^{a}(\sin(\theta))^{2b+1}\cos(\theta)
=2​(1−sin2⁡(θ))a​(sin⁡(θ))2​b+1​cos⁡(θ).\displaystyle=2(1-\sin^{2}(\theta))^{a}(\sin(\theta))^{2b+1}\cos(\theta).

The substitution u=sin⁡(θ)u=\sin(\theta) gives us

∫0π/2cos2​a⁡(θ)​sin2​b⁡(θ)​sin⁡(2​θ)​𝑑θ\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\cos^{2a}(\theta)\sin^{2b}(\theta)\sin(2\theta)\,{\mathrm{d}}\theta =∫012​(1−u2)a​u2​b+1​𝑑u\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{1}2(1-u^{2})^{a}u^{2b+1}\,{\mathrm{d}}u
=∫01(1−u2)a​(u2)b​(2​u​𝑑u)\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{1}(1-u^{2})^{a}(u^{2})^{b}(2u\,{\mathrm{d}}u)
=∫01(1−t)a​tb​𝑑t.\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{1}(1-t)^{a}t^{b}\,{\mathrm{d}}t.

The desired identity now follows from Identity B.1. ∎

Identity B.5.

For nonnegative integers a,b,c,da,b,c,d, we have

∫SU2⁡(ℂ)u11a​u12b​u21c​u22d={(−1)b​a!​b!(a+b+1)!if a=d and b=c,0else.\int_{\SU_{2}(\mathbb{C})}u_{11}^{a}u_{12}^{b}u_{21}^{c}u_{22}^{d}=\begin{cases}(-1)^{b}\dfrac{a!b!}{(a+b+1)!}&\text{if $a=d$ and $b=c$},\\[3.0pt] 0&\text{else}.\end{cases}
Proof.

We use the formula for the Haar measure on SU2⁡(ℂ)\SU_{2}(\mathbb{C}) from [Fa, Proposition 7.4.1]. Given a smooth function f:SU2⁡(ℂ)-→ℂf\colon\SU_{2}(\mathbb{C})\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\meno}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\meno}$}}}\mathrel{\mkern-3.0mu}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}, we have

∫SU2⁡(ℂ)f\displaystyle\int_{\SU_{2}(\mathbb{C})}f =12​π2​∫0π/2∫0π∫−ππf⁡([eι​ψe−ι​ψ]​[cos⁡(θ)sin⁡(θ)−sin⁡(θ)cos⁡(θ)]​[eι​φe−ι​φ])​sin⁡(2​θ)​𝑑ψ​𝑑φ​𝑑θ\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2\pi^{2}}\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\int_{0}^{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}f\left(\begin{bmatrix}e^{\iota\psi}&\\ &e^{-\iota\psi}\\ \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\cos(\theta)&\sin(\theta)\\ -\sin(\theta)&\cos(\theta)\\ \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}e^{\iota\varphi}&\\ &e^{-\iota\varphi}\\ \end{bmatrix}\right)\sin(2\theta)\,{\mathrm{d}}\psi\,{\mathrm{d}}\varphi\,{\mathrm{d}}\theta
=12​π2​∫0π/2∫0π∫−ππf⁡([eι⁡(ψ+φ)​cos⁡(θ)eι⁡(ψ−φ)​sin⁡(θ)−eι⁡(−ψ+φ)​sin⁡(θ)eι⁡(−ψ−φ)​cos⁡(θ)])​sin⁡(2​θ)​𝑑ψ​𝑑φ​𝑑θ.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2\pi^{2}}\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\int_{0}^{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}f\left(\begin{bmatrix}e^{\iota(\psi+\varphi)}\cos(\theta)&e^{\iota(\psi-\varphi)}\sin(\theta)\\ -e^{\iota(-\psi+\varphi)}\sin(\theta)&e^{\iota(-\psi-\varphi)}\cos(\theta)\\ \end{bmatrix}\right)\sin(2\theta)\,{\mathrm{d}}\psi\,{\mathrm{d}}\varphi\,{\mathrm{d}}\theta.

Rewriting in terms of the above coordinates, we get

u11a​u12b​u21c​u22d=(−1)c​exp⁡(ι​ψ​(a+b−c−d))​exp⁡(ι​φ​(a−b+c−d))​cosa+d⁡(θ)​sinb+c⁡(θ).u_{11}^{a}u_{12}^{b}u_{21}^{c}u_{22}^{d}=(-1)^{c}\exp(\iota\psi(a+b-c-d))\exp(\iota\varphi(a-b+c-d))\cos^{a+d}(\theta)\sin^{b+c}(\theta).

We integrate using Fubini’s theorem to obtain

2​π2​∫SU2⁡(ℂ)u11a​u12b​u21c​u22d\displaystyle 2\pi^{2}\int_{\SU_{2}(\mathbb{C})}u_{11}^{a}u_{12}^{b}u_{21}^{c}u_{22}^{d}
=(−1)c⋅∫−ππexp⁡(ι​ψ​(a+b−c−d))​𝑑ψ⋅∫0πexp⁡(ι​φ​(a−b+c−d))​𝑑φ⋅∫0π/2cosa+d⁡(θ)​sinb+c⁡(θ)​sin⁡(2​θ)​𝑑θ.\displaystyle=(-1)^{c}\cdot\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\exp(\iota\psi(a+b-c-d))\,{\mathrm{d}}\psi\cdot\int_{0}^{\pi}\exp(\iota\varphi(a-b+c-d))\,{\mathrm{d}}\varphi\cdot\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\cos^{a+d}(\theta)\sin^{b+c}(\theta)\sin(2\theta)\,{\mathrm{d}}\theta.

For the first integral to be nonzero, we must have a+b−c−d=0a+b-c-d=0. This implies that a−b+c−da-b+c-d is even and hence must be zero if the second integral is to be nonzero. Solving these two equations simultaneously gives us a=da=d and b=cb=c. Assume now that these two equations hold. We then have

2​π2​∫SU2⁡(ℂ)u11a​u12b​u21c​u22d\displaystyle 2\pi^{2}\int_{\SU_{2}(\mathbb{C})}u_{11}^{a}u_{12}^{b}u_{21}^{c}u_{22}^{d}
=(−1)b⋅∫−ππ1​𝑑ψ⋅∫0π1​𝑑φ⋅∫0π/2cos2​a⁡(θ)​sin2​b⁡(θ)​sin⁡(2​θ)​𝑑θ\displaystyle=(-1)^{b}\cdot\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}1\,{\mathrm{d}}\psi\cdot\int_{0}^{\pi}1\,{\mathrm{d}}\varphi\cdot\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\cos^{2a}(\theta)\sin^{2b}(\theta)\sin(2\theta)\,{\mathrm{d}}\theta
=(−1)b​(2​π2)⋅a!​b!(a+b+1)!,\displaystyle=(-1)^{b}(2\pi^{2})\cdot\frac{a!b!}{(a+b+1)!},

where the last equality follows from Identity B.4. ∎
